newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Prices seen holding.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Prices seen holding.

text.p: Healthy demand for some products and the effect of cuts in refinery runs are expected to keep Asian oil products prices steady this week after a mild recovery, traders said on Monday.
Leading the pack are jet fuel and gasoline which are enjoying rising prices as supplies are mopped up by growing demand, traders said.

They said jet fuel supplies were tight on a combination of factors -- active buying from Indonesia for February, cargo movements from Northeast Asia to the U.S. West Coast and a trader pushing up prices.
After seeing a deal done as high as $30.75 on Thursday, three buyers appeared at $31.00-$31.30.
Traders said jet fuel prices would continue to climb this week before consolidating as demand is expected to remain healthy until first half of March.
They said the recent surge in jet prices has made it uneconomical to move cargoes to the U.S. West Coast.

The gasoline market is supported by demand from India and low stocks in Singapore. Light distillate stocks fell 233,000 barrels to 5.19 million barrels for the week ended January 29, the lowest in two months.
The shortfall was also due to refineries cutting reforming runs, sources said.
India is seeking a total of 100,000 tonnes 87-octane leaded gasoline for March to compensate for the 30-day shutdown at an 18,000-barrel-per-day catalytic cracker in Bombay next month.
India's demand has prompted a trader to move gasoline cargoes to the Middle East for blending to meet the subcontinent's requirements.
Traders see 95-octane gasoline at $26.40/$27.20 on Friday and is expected to continue to rise in the short term.
Despite slow regional demand and ample fuel oil supplies in Singapore and South Korea, the market appeared to resist a sharp fall largely due to strong buying interest on the swaps market.
On Friday, 180-centistoke fuel oil was discussed at $97.50, down slightly from previous week, while swaps were traded at $100.50.

Traders said the market was expecting the cuts in refinery runs to help absorb surplus fuel oil cargoes and support prices. Only gas oil remained in the doldrums, despite attempts by a major to support prices above $26.00 per barrel and a recovery during the week in London gas oil futures.

A wet deal was done on Friday at $25.30 between a Singapore trader and a European major for a second-half February lifting cargo. But one trader said that a few players were trying to push prices lower despite surplus stocks being cleared up.
Traders also said the strong crude prices were forcing refining margins to remain in the red despite the cut in refining runs and the strong jet fuel and gasoline prices.
Other areas of focus:
* LSWR waiting for final details on Indonesia's February export allocations. Traders expect allocation of around 3.7 million barrels versus January's 3.5 million barrels.
* Taiwan's tender to buy two 38,000-tonne cargoes of 0.5 percent sulphur fuel oil for delivery between February and March closes February 3, valid two days.
* India tenders to buy 40-45,000 tonne cargoes of 0.5-pct sulphur diesel for March 1-5 and March 16-20, delivered to Kandla. The tender closes Feb 5.
